AlberdiLab | Fix et al 2025 Brush-tail possum metagenomics Lukas Fix, Antton Alberdi, Raphael Eisenhofer Last update: 2026-11-17 Chapter 1 Introduction This webbook contains the analysis code for the brushtail possum (Trichosurus vulpecula) metagenomics study (Fix et al.; Ecology Letters Letter target). The manuscript asks how Tasmanian devil density, ambient temperature, and their interaction shape gut MAG abundances and genome-inferred functional traits (GIFTs), with land-cover diversity and sequencing depth as covariates. Sample accounting (matches the manuscript and data/archive_deposit/): 73 faecal samples collected; 1 mainland sample failed QC → 72 in the MAG catalogue (1,817 non-redundant MAGs). 55 Tasmanian samples from 17 sites enter HMSC; 17 mainland samples stay in the catalogue only (not in HMSC). HMSC response: 55 × 576 genomes (pinned list data/model_final_genomes.tsv). Coverage rule for presence/diversity: CoverM ≥ 30% genome covered (min_coverage = 0.3). HMSC formula: devil + temperature + devil:temperature + diversity + logseqdepth, with site and animal random effects; Gaussian responses; posterior support ≥ 0.90. MCMC: deposited hmsc/Hmsc_model_final.rds has 4 chains × 250 samples (verified). Launch/import path uses thin = 1000, transient 250,000 (13_ / 14_ / launch_hmsc_model_final.sh). Slurm .out logs are not in this repo; see Paper manuscript/MCMC_PROVENANCE.md. GIFT class contrasts: Welch t-tests + BH FDR (see ch14 / R/plot_helpers.R). Upstream assembly/binning (EHI Snakemake: metaSPAdes, dRep 98% ANI, CoverM, GTDB-Tk, DRAM) is documented in the manuscript Methods; this webbook starts from the deposited count, coverage, taxonomy, GIFT and environmental tables. Manuscript figures (Ecology Letters): Fig. 1 catalogue + Tasmanian diversity; Fig. 2 maps/environment + phylo–GIFT; Fig. 3 HMSC functional contrasts + prediction. Chapter 15 still also exports exploratory multi-panel IDs (A–G / F-series) used during figure development—treat paper Figs 1–3 as the submission set. Chapter 2 Prepare data 2.1 Load data 2.2 load_read_counts 2.3 load_genome_metadata 2.4 Genome base hits 2.5 Genome tree 2.6 Genome annotations 2.7 Filter reads by coverage 2.8 Transform reads into genome counts 2.9 Prepare color scheme 2.10 Wrap working objects

Chapter 2 Prepare data We load pipeline outputs and metadata, harmonise identifiers, and derive working objects used downstream: coverage-filtered counts, genome lengths and phylogeny, genome annotations (via Airtable), colour palettes, and GIFT-based functional tables. Everything is wrapped as a single RData for reuse. 2.1 Load data Load the original data files outputted by the bioinformatic pipeline. 2.1.1 Sample metadata Note: Load sample metadata from the merged metadata file. The first column is renamed to “sample” to ensure consistent naming across the analysis. outlier_sample <- "EHI01340" sample_metadata <- read_tsv("data/merged_metadata.tsv") %>% rename(sample=1) %>% filter(sample != outlier_sample) sample_sites <- readr::read_csv("data/sample_sites.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) sample_metadata <- sample_metadata %>% left_join(sample_sites, by = c("sample" = "id")) valid_samples <- sample_metadata$sample 2.2 load_read_counts Note: Load read count data from the compressed TSV file. Rename the first column to “genome” and select only columns corresponding to samples present in the metadata. This ensures data consistency between counts and metadata. read_counts <- read_tsv("data/DMB0167_counts.tsv.gz") %>% rename(genome=1) %>% select(any_of(c("genome", valid_samples))) 2.3 load_genome_metadata Note: Load genome metadata (MAG information) from the compressed TSV file. Rename “mag_size” to “length” for consistency. Filter to only include genomes present in the read counts data and arrange them in the same order as read_counts to ensure alignment across datasets. genome_metadata <- read_tsv("data/DMB0167_mag_info.tsv.gz") %>% rename(length=mag_size)%>% semi_join(., read_counts, by = "genome") %>% arrange(match(genome,read_counts$genome)) 2.4 Genome base hits Note: Load genome coverage data (base hits) from the compressed TSV file. Rename the first column to “genome”, select only columns for samples in metadata, filter to genomes present in genome_metadata, and arrange in the same order as read_counts. This coverage data is used to filter low-coverage genomes. genome_coverage <- read_tsv("data/DMB0167_coverage.tsv.gz") %>% rename(genome=1) %>% select(any_of(c("genome", valid_samples))) %>% semi_join(., genome_metadata, by = "genome") %>% arrange(match(genome, read_counts$genome)) 2.5 Genome tree Note: Load the phylogenetic tree of genomes from the compressed Newick file. Remove single quotes from tip labels (MAG names) and prune the tree to only include tips corresponding to genomes in the metadata. This ensures the tree matches the genomes used in downstream analyses. genome_tree <- read_tree("data/DMB0167.tree.gz") genome_tree$tip.label <- str_replace_all(genome_tree$tip.label,"'", "") #remove single quotes in MAG names genome_tree <- keep.tip(genome_tree, tip=genome_metadata$genome) # keep only MAG tips 2.6 Genome annotations Note: Download genome annotation files from ERDA using Airtable metadata. This chunk connects to Airtable, retrieves annotation URLs for MAGs with genes, downloads all annotation tables, and combines them into a single compressed file. This only needs to be run once to generate the genome_annotations table. Note that the Airtable connection requires a personal access token. anno_file <- "data/genome_annotations.tsv.xz" if (file.exists(anno_file)) { message("Using existing genome annotations: ", anno_file) } else { airtable("MAGs", "appWbHBNLE6iAsMRV") %>% #get base ID from Airtable browser URL read_airtable(., fields = c("ID","mag_name","number_genes","anno_url"), id_to_col = TRUE) %>% #get 3 columns from MAGs table filter(mag_name %in% paste0(genome_metadata$genome,".fa")) %>% #filter by MAG name filter(number_genes > 0) %>% #genes need to exist select(anno_url) %>% #list MAG annotation urls pull() %>% read_tsv() %>% #load all tables rename(gene=1, genome=2, contig=3) %>% #rename first 3 columns write_tsv(file = anno_file) #write to overall compressed file } Note: Load the pre-generated genome annotations table from the compressed file. Rename the first three columns to “gene”, “genome”, and “contig” for consistency. This annotation data is used for functional analysis using the GIFT framework. genome_annotations <- read_tsv("data/genome_annotations.tsv.xz") %>% rename(gene=1, genome=2, contig=3) 2.7 Filter reads by coverage Note: Filter read counts based on genome coverage. Set minimum coverage threshold (0.3) and create a binary mask where genomes with coverage above the threshold are kept (1) and below are excluded (0). Multiply read counts by this mask to zero out reads from low-coverage genomes, ensuring only high-quality genome assignments are retained. min_coverage=0.3 sample_cols <- setdiff(names(read_counts), "genome") coverage_mask <- genome_coverage %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ ifelse(. > min_coverage, 1, 0))) read_counts_filt <- read_counts %>% left_join( coverage_mask %>% rename_with(~ paste0(.x, "_mask"), -genome), by = "genome" ) read_counts_filt[sample_cols] <- read_counts_filt[sample_cols] * read_counts_filt[paste0(sample_cols, "_mask")] read_counts_filt <- read_counts_filt %>% select(genome, all_of(sample_cols)) 2.8 Transform reads into genome counts Note: Transform raw read counts into normalized genome counts by dividing by genome length (scaled by read length). This accounts for the fact that longer genomes will naturally have more reads mapped to them, normalizing counts to represent relative abundance rather than absolute read numbers. readlength <- 150 genome_length_lookup <- genome_metadata %>% select(genome, mag_length = length) genome_counts <- read_counts %>% left_join(genome_length_lookup, by = "genome") %>% mutate(across(-c(genome, mag_length), ~ . / (mag_length / readlength))) %>% select(-mag_length) Note: Transform filtered read counts (after coverage filtering) into normalized genome counts using the same length normalization approach. This creates the filtered genome count matrix used in downstream analyses, excluding low-coverage genomes. readlength <- 150 genome_counts_filt <- read_counts_filt %>% left_join(genome_length_lookup, by = "genome") %>% mutate(across(-c(genome, mag_length), ~ . / (mag_length / readlength))) %>% select(-mag_length) 2.8.1 Distill annotations into GIFTs Note: Convert genome annotations into GIFT (Genome-Inferred Functional Traits) format using the distillR package. This aggregates gene-level annotations into functional trait profiles for each genome, which are used for community-level functional analysis. The function processes annotations from columns 9, 10, and 19 of the annotation table. genome_gifts <- distill(genome_annotations,GIFT_db,genomecol=2,annotcol=c(9,10,19), verbosity=F) 2.9 Prepare color scheme Note: Load phylum-level color scheme from the EHI taxonomy color repository. Join with genome metadata to get colors for phyla present in the dataset, arrange to match the tree tip order, and create a named vector mapping phylum names to colors. This ensures consistent color coding across all visualizations. phylum_colors <- read_tsv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/earthhologenome/EHI_taxonomy_colour/main/ehi_phylum_colors.tsv") %>% right_join(genome_metadata, by=join_by(phylum == phylum)) %>% arrange(match(genome, genome_tree$tip.label)) %>% select(phylum, colors) %>% unique() %>% arrange(phylum) %>% pull(colors, name=phylum) Note: Classify samples into geographic regions (Tasmania vs Australia) based on latitude and longitude coordinates. Samples within the specified geographic bounds are classified as “Tasmania”, all others as “Australia”. This creates a categorical variable for geographic analysis. sample_metadata <- sample_metadata %>% mutate( island = case_when( latitude < -38 & latitude > -45 & longitude > 140 & longitude < 150 ~ "Tasmania", TRUE ~ "Australia" ) ) 2.10 Wrap working objects Note: Save all processed data objects into a single RData file for efficient loading in downstream analyses. This includes sample metadata, genome metadata, read counts, normalized genome counts (both filtered and unfiltered), phylogenetic tree, GIFT functional annotations, and color schemes. All subsequent chapters load this single file to access the prepared data. eval = FALSE for routine webbook renders: distill_annotations above is also off (heavy), and a current data/data.Rdata is already in the repo. Re-enable this chunk only after re-running annotation download + distill locally. save(sample_metadata, genome_metadata, read_counts, genome_counts, genome_counts_filt, genome_tree, genome_gifts, phylum_colors, file = "data/data.Rdata")

Compute these fractions for each sample and convert to gigabases. Display mean ± SD in gigabases sequence_fractions %>% mutate(across(-sample, ~ . / 1000000000)) %>% summarise(across(where(is.numeric), list(mean = \(x) round(mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), 2), sd = \(x) round(sd(x, na.rm = TRUE), 2)), .names = "{.col}_{.fn}")) %>% pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c("fraction", ".value"), names_pattern = "(.+)_(mean|sd)") %>% unite("GB", mean, sd, sep = " ± ") %>% mutate(fraction = factor(fraction, levels = c("lowqual_bases", "host_bases", "unmapped_bases", "mags_bases"), labels = c("Low quality", "Mapped to host", "Unmapped", "Mapped to MAGs"))) %>% arrange(fraction) %>% rename("Category" = fraction) %>% tt() # Chapter 4 MAG catalogue An overview of the recovered MAGs: circular phylogeny with phylum ring, genome quality and size rings, and “new species” flags; summaries of MAG sizes and quality; and a high-level functional overview including a t-SNE of genome functions. 4.1 Microbiota data Note: Load all required data objects including genome metadata, phylogenetic tree, GIFT annotations, and color schemes from the RData file created in the data preparation chapter. load("data/data.Rdata") Note: Filter out sample EHI01340 from the metadata. This sample was removed because it could not be mapped to MAGs, ensuring consistency across downstream analyses. sample_metadata<- sample_metadata %>% filter(sample!="EHI01340") EHI01340 sample has been removed because of inability to map MAGS 4.1.1 Genome phylogeny Circular phylogeny of MAGs with four rings: phylum (outer heatmap), genome quality (bar, completeness filled by contamination), ‘new species’ flag, and genome size. Labels indicate ring meaning; tree ultrametricised for visualisation. Note: Prepare data for circular phylogenetic tree visualization. This sample was removed because it could not be mapped to MAGs, ensuring consistency across downstream analyses. sample_metadata <- sample_metadata %>% dplyr::filter(sample != "EHI01340") hill_long <- hill_long %>% dplyr::filter(id != "EHI01340") Note: Transform Hill diversity data from long to wide format, creating separate columns for each Hill diversity metric (env_hill_h0, env_hill_h1, env_hill_h2). Join with sample metadata to create a combined metadata object for downstream analyses. 11.3 Helper functions Note: Helper function to align metadata with distance matrices. This eliminates code duplication when aligning metadata for multiple distance matrices. Defined early as it’s needed by multiple analysis sections. Note: Optimized helper function that accepts pre-calculated NMDS object instead of recalculating. This eliminates redundant NMDS calculations when creating multiple plots. 11.4 Ordination analysis Note: Extract distance matrices from beta diversity objects for use in ordination analyses. These matrices represent Bray-Curtis dissimilarities between samples at different diversity orders. Note: Calculate all NMDS ordinations once upfront. These are expensive operations (trymax = 500 iterations each) and were previously calculated redundantly 3+ times. This optimization saves significant computation time. Note: Align metadata with each distance matrix using the helper function. This ensures proper sample order matching for ordination and visualization. 11.5 Grouping variables Note: Create grouping variables for environmental Hill diversity metrics. Calculate medians once to avoid redundant calculations. Split into tertiles (Low, Mid, High) and median-based groups (Low, High) for visualization and statistical testing. Note: Verify the grouping variables were created correctly by displaying frequency tables. This ensures balanced group sizes for downstream analyses. 11.6 PERMANOVA analysis Note: Define function to run PERMANOVA tests for each environmental Hill diversity metric (h0, h1, h2) against beta diversity distance matrices. The function aligns metadata with distance matrix samples, ensures sample order matches, and performs PERMANOVA with 999 permutations for each Hill metric. This eliminates code duplication when testing multiple beta diversity matrices. 11.7 Mantel tests Note: Test correlations between environmental Hill diversity and beta diversity using Mantel tests. This is more appropriate than linear regression on NMDS axes since it tests relationships directly on distance matrices, which is the appropriate scale for beta diversity analysis. 11.8 Betadisper tests Note: Test for homogeneity of multivariate dispersions (variance) across Hill diversity tertile groups using betadisper. This tests whether groups differ in their dispersion around the centroid, which is an assumption of PERMANOVA. Tests all three beta diversity matrices for consistency. 11.9 Correlation tests Note: Test correlations between environmental Hill diversity variables and NMDS ordination axes using Spearman correlation. This is more appropriate than linear regression for non-metric ordination and provides correlation coefficients and significance tests. 11.10 Visualization Associations between environmental α-diversity (Hill h0/h1/h2) and microbiome ordination (NMDS1/2), with fitted vectors and a subset heatmap of Bray–Curtis distances. For each q value, create filtered metadata and genome count matrices containing only samples in Low/High groups and genomes present in at least one sample. 12.3 Structural zeros analysis Note: Identify structural zeros - genomes that are completely absent (zero counts) in one group (Low or High) but present in the other. This is important for ANCOM-BC2 analysis as structural zeros can be handled explicitly. For each q value, calculate which genomes are structurally absent in Low vs High groups and compute group means for genomes that are present in only one group. Note: Create UpSet plot using UpSetR to visualize the intersection of genomes present in Low and High environmental diversity groups. The plot shows unique genomes in each group and shared genomes, with colors indicating group membership. 12.4 Differential abundance analysis 12.4.1 Build phyloseq objects Note: Create phyloseq objects for each q value (q0, q1, q2) containing OTU table (genome counts), taxonomy table, and sample metadata. Counts are kept as integers with zeros allowed, as ANCOM-BC2 can handle zeros without requiring pseudocounts. Sample metadata includes the grouping variable (Low/High) for each Hill diversity metric. 12.4.2 Run ANCOM-BC2 analysis Note: Perform ANCOM-BC2 differential abundance testing for each q value, comparing Low vs High environmental diversity groups. The analysis uses structural zero modeling (struc_zero=TRUE) to properly handle genomes absent in one group. Version-adaptive code handles differences between ANCOMBC package versions. Results include log fold-changes, p-values, and adjusted p-values for each genome. 12.4.3 Visualize differential abundance results Note: Extract significantly differentially abundant genomes (p < 0.05) from ANCOM-BC2 results and create visualizations. Barplots show log2 fold-changes for significant genomes, ordered by effect size and colored by phylum. Volcano plots show all tested genomes with log2 fold-change on x-axis and -log10(p-value) on y-axis, highlighting significant hits. Both visualizations are created for each q value (q0, q1, q2). Note: Alternative barplot visualization using genome identifiers instead of taxon names. This provides a different view of the same differential abundance results, useful for identifying specific genomes of interest. 12.5 Alternative ANCOM-BC2 analysis with structural zeros Note: Run an alternative ANCOM-BC2 analysis with additional structural zero handling parameters. This analysis uses a random effects model (rand_formula=“~1”) and different parameter settings including Holm p-value adjustment, pseudo-sensitivity analysis, and explicit structural zero detection. This provides a complementary view to the primary ANCOM-BC2 analysis in this exploratory chapter (not part of the Letter Methods) and may identify additional differentially abundant genomes. Note: Extract and clean results from the alternative ANCOM-BC2 analysis with structural zeros. Filter for significantly differentially abundant genomes (p < 0.05), join with taxonomy information, and create cleaned tables ready for visualization or further analysis. Results are organized by log fold-change for easy interpretation. 12.6 Load data Note: Load sample metadata, genome count data, and Hill diversity metrics from RData files created in previous chapters. These data objects will be used for diversity and abundance analysis comparing samples with low and high environmental diversity. 12.7 Data preparation Note: Exclude outlier sample EHI01340 from all datasets. Transform Hill diversity data from long to wide format and join with sample metadata. Choose a Hill diversity metric (default: h1, exponential Shannon) to split samples into tertiles. Filter to keep only Low and High groups (excluding Mid) for two-group comparisons. Check sample_metadata.") } if (nrow(genome_counts_filt) == 0) { stop("Error: No genomes remaining after filtering. Check genome_counts_filt.") } # --- choose which Hill order to split on ---------------------------------- # use "h1" by default (exp-Shannon). Change to "h0" or "h2" if you prefer. q_choice <- "h1" # Validate q_choice format valid_q_choices <- c("h0", "h1", "h2") if (!q_choice %in% valid_q_choices) { stop("Error: q_choice must be one of: ", paste(valid_q_choices, collapse = ", ")) } # Validate hill_long exists and has data if (!exists("hill_long") || nrow(hill_long) == 0) { stop("Error: hill_long is missing or empty.") } # Optimized: Build Hill-wide and join with metadata in one pipeline hill_col <- paste0("env_hill_", q_choice) hill_wide <- hill_long %>% filter(id != outlier_sample) %>% rename(sample = id) %>% pivot_wider(id_cols = sample, names_from = q, values_from = value, names_glue = "env_hill_{q}") # Validate pivot_wider results if (!hill_col %in% colnames(hill_wide)) { stop("Error: Hill diversity column '", hill_col, "' not found after pivot_wider. ", "Available columns: ", paste(colnames(hill_wide), collapse = ", ")) } # Optimized: Join and filter missing Hill data in one step meta_hill <- sample_metadata %>% left_join(hill_wide, by = "sample") %>% filter(!is.na(.data[[hill_col]])) # Remove samples with missing Hill diversity data # Report if any samples were excluded n_excluded_hill <- nrow(sample_metadata) - nrow(meta_hill) if (n_excluded_hill > 0) { warning("Found ", n_excluded_hill, " samples with missing Hill diversity data. Need at least 3 samples.") } group_col <- paste0("env_group_q", substr(q_choice, 2, 2)) # env_group_q1, etc. # tertiles → keep only Low/High (drop Mid) and fix factor order Low < High # Use tryCatch to handle edge cases in cut_number meta_hill <- tryCatch({ meta_hill %>% mutate( !!group_col := ggplot2::cut_number(.data[[hill_col]], 3, labels = c("Low","Mid","High")) ) %>% filter(.data[[group_col]] %in% c("Low","High")) %>% mutate(!!group_col := factor(.data[[group_col]], levels = c("Low","High"))) }, error = function(e) { stop("Error creating tertiles with cut_number: ", e$message, ". ", paste(names(group_counts), group_counts, sep = "=", collapse = ", ")) } # Optimized: Keep only samples present in both datasets in one pass valid_samples <- intersect(meta_hill$sample, colnames(genome_counts_filt)) if (length(valid_samples) == 0) { stop("Error: No overlapping samples between meta_hill and genome_counts_filt.") } # Filter both datasets to valid samples meta_hill <- meta_hill %>% filter(sample %in% valid_samples) genome_counts_filt <- genome_counts_filt %>% select(genome, all_of(valid_samples)) %>% # Re-filter genomes to ensure they're still present after sample filtering filter(rowSums(across(-genome, ~ .x != 0), na.rm = TRUE) > 0) # Final validation if (nrow(meta_hill) == 0) { stop("Error: No samples remaining after final filtering.") } cat("N Low / High = ", sum(meta_hill[[group_col]] == "Low"), " / ", sum(meta_hill[[group_col]] == "High"), "\n", sep = "") 12.8 Structural zeros analysis Note: Identify structural zeros - genomes that are completely absent (zero counts) in one group (Low or High) but present in the other. Chapter 13 HMSC final model setup This chapter defines the definitive HMSC model for downstream analyses. The model is restricted to Tasmania samples, uses 200 m environmental buffers, and includes a devil × temperature interaction term. library(tidyverse) library(Hmsc) library(ape) 13.1 Load data source("R/chapter_deps.R") load("data/data.Rdata") ensure_hmsc_env_csvs() animal_variables <- read_csv("data/animal_var.csv") location_variables <- read_csv("data/environment_var_r200.csv") predictors <- inner_join(animal_variables, location_variables, by = "id") %>% rename(sample = id) %>% filter(sample %in% sample_metadata$sample[sample_metadata$island == "Tasmania"]) 13.2 Filter genomes The genome set is pinned in data/model_final_genomes.tsv (576 genomes) so it matches the fitted model on ERDA. Do not re-derive this list from prevalence filters unless you intend to refit the model on HPC. (A simple “>10% of samples and >5 sites” rule on the current Tasmania table does not regenerate this list; the manuscript therefore cites the pinned genome set rather than that filter.) genomes_to_model <- read_tsv("data/model_final_genomes.tsv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>% pull(genome) 13.3 Build model inputs StudyDesign <- predictors %>% select(sample, site) %>% mutate(animal = sample) %>% mutate(animal = factor(animal), site = factor(site)) %>% column_to_rownames("sample") normalisation_factors <- genome_metadata %>% mutate(norm_factor = median(length) / length) %>% select(genome, norm_factor) YData <- read_counts %>% left_join(normalisation_factors, by = "genome") %>% mutate(across(-c(genome, norm_factor), ~ round(. * norm_factor, 0))) %>% select(-norm_factor) %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ . + 1)) %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ log(.))) %>% filter(genome %in% genomes_to_model) %>% column_to_rownames("genome") %>% select(all_of(row.names(StudyDesign))) %>% as.data.frame() %>% t() XData <- predictors %>% select(sample, temperature, precipitation, diversity, density, devil) %>% mutate(logseqdepth = read_counts %>% select(all_of(row.names(StudyDesign))) %>% colSums() %>% log()) %>% column_to_rownames("sample") PData <- genome_tree %>% keep.tip(tip = genomes_to_model) 13.4 Model formula XFormula = ~ devil + temperature + diversity + logseqdepth + devil:temperature rL.animal = HmscRandomLevel(units = levels(StudyDesign$animal)) rL.site = HmscRandomLevel(units = levels(StudyDesign$site)) 13.5 Define and save unfitted model The unfitted model object is saved as hmsc/model_final. The version in the repository (55 Tasmania samples, 576 genomes) is the canonical model for fitting and analysis. Re-running the chunks above may produce a different genome set because filtering was tuned for the final model; only rebuild if you intend to replace hmsc/model_final deliberately. # eval=FALSE for webbook renders — do not overwrite the canonical hmsc/model_final object. m = Hmsc( Y = YData, XData = XData, XFormula = XFormula, studyDesign = StudyDesign, phyloTree = PData, ranLevels = list("animal" = rL.animal, "site" = rL.site), distr = "normal", YScale = TRUE ) save(m, file = "hmsc/model_final") 13.6 In the HPC The commands below are for the HPC cluster only. They are shown for reference and are not executed when knitting this book locally. The launch script is also saved as launch_hmsc_model_final.sh in the project root. 13.6.1 Prepare the initiation object conda activate hmsc-hpc model="hmsc/model_final" init="init/model_final.rds" export samples=250 export thin=1000 export transient=$(( samples * thin )) # nChains=4 is the intended design (four independent sampler jobs / posterior lists). # The single-process hmsc.run_gibbs_sampler call below fits one chain; run four jobs # (or pass the engine-specific chain flag if your Hmsc-HPC build exposes one) and combine. export nChains=4 export verbose=TRUE export model export init # Get initiation object (hmsc.r must be available on the HPC) Rscript hmsc.r $model $init 13.6.2 Launch script cat <<'EOF' > launch_hmsc_model_final.sh #!/bin/bash #SBATCH --job-name=hmsc_model_final #SBATCH --nodes=1 #SBATCH --partition=cpuqueue #SBATCH --qos=normal #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1 #SBATCH --ntasks=1 #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1 #SBATCH --mem=32gb #SBATCH --time=150:00:00 # Activate conda environment source activate hmsc-hpc # Set output files output="output/Hmsc_model_final.rds" mkdir output # One chain per job. Submit four jobs (or array 0-3) for nChains=4; $nChains is documentation only here. srun python3 -m hmsc.run_gibbs_sampler --input $init --output $output --samples $samples --transient $transient --thin $thin --verbose 100 EOF 13.6.3 Submit job sbatch launch_hmsc_model_final.sh

Chapter 14 HMSC final model analysis This chapter loads the fitted model_final posterior from ERDA, runs variance partitioning and association analyses, and writes data/publication_hmsc.Rdata for chapter 15 (publication figures). library(tidyverse) library(Hmsc) library(ape) library(distillR) library(ggrepel) library(forcats) 14.1 Load data Note: Load the main data file containing sample metadata, genome counts, genome metadata, phylogenetic tree, and other required objects. Canonical fit settings (must match the manuscript and launch_hmsc_model_final.sh): nSamples=250, thin=1000, transient=250000, nChains=4, support_threshold=0.9. GIFT class contrasts below use Welch t.test + BH FDR (not Wilcoxon). #Parameters nSamples=250 thin=1000 transient=nSamples * thin support_threshold=0.9 negsupport_threshold=1-support_threshold 14.3 Helper functions Note: Define reusable helper functions to extract beta estimates, support values, and credible intervals from HMSC models. These functions eliminate code duplication and ensure consistent extraction patterns across all analyses. # Safe correlation function that checks dimensions safe_cor <- function(x, y, ...) { if (length(x) != length(y)) { warning(paste("Vectors have incompatible dimensions:", length(x), "vs", length(y), ". Returning NA.")) return(NA) } if (length(x) == 0) { return(NA) } tryCatch({ cor(x, y, ...) }, error = function(e) { warning(paste("Error computing correlation:", e$message)) return(NA) }) } # Extract beta mean estimate for a specific covariate get_beta_estimate <- function(fit_model_18, model_obj, covariate_name) { getPostEstimate(hM = fit_model_18, parName = "Beta")$mean %>% as.data.frame() %>% mutate(variable = model_obj$covNames) %>% filter(variable == covariate_name) %>% pivot_longer(!variable, names_to = "genome", values_to = "mean") %>% dplyr::select(genome, mean) } # Extract beta support values for a specific covariate get_beta_support <- function(fit_model_18, model_obj, covariate_name) { getPostEstimate(hM = fit_model_18, parName = "Beta")$support %>% as.data.frame() %>% mutate(variable = model_obj$covNames) %>% filter(variable == covariate_name) %>% pivot_longer(!variable, names_to = "genome", values_to = "support") %>% dplyr::select(genome, support) } # Extract beta credible intervals for a specific covariate get_beta_ci <- function(fit_model_18, model_obj, covariate_name, quantiles = c(0.1, 0.9)) { beta_q <- getPostEstimate(hM = fit_model_18, parName = "Beta", q = quantiles)$q idx_cov <- which(model_obj$covNames == covariate_name) n_genomes <- length(model_obj$spNames) purrr::map_dfr(1:n_genomes, ~ { tibble( genome = model_obj$spNames[.x], q10 = beta_q[1, idx_cov, .x], q90 = beta_q[2, idx_cov, .x] ) }) } # Combine beta estimate, support, and credible intervals with metadata get_beta_complete <- function(fit_model_18, model_obj, covariate_name, quantiles = c(0.1, 0.9)) { estimate <- get_beta_estimate(fit_model_18, model_obj, covariate_name) ci <- get_beta_ci(fit_model_18, model_obj, covariate_name, quantiles) ci %>% right_join(estimate, by = "genome") %>% left_join(genome_metadata, by = "genome") } # Calculate functional differences between positive and negative associations calculate_functional_differences <- function(elements_response, variable_name) { var_sym <- rlang::sym(variable_name) elements_response %>% filter(!!var_sym != "Neutral") %>% mutate(!!var_sym := droplevels(!!var_sym)) %>% group_by(GIFT) %>% summarise( n_pos = sum(!!var_sym == "Positive"), n_neg = sum(!!var_sym == "Negative"), mean_pos = mean(value[!!var_sym == "Positive"], na.rm = TRUE), mean_neg = mean(value[!!var_sym == "Negative"], na.rm = TRUE), diff = mean_pos - mean_neg, p = if (n_pos > 1 && n_neg > 1 && stats::sd(value[!!var_sym == "Positive"], na.rm = TRUE) > 0 && stats::sd(value[!!var_sym == "Negative"], na.rm = TRUE) > 0) { stats::t.test(value ~ !!var_sym, var.equal = FALSE)$p.value } else NA_real_, .groups = "drop" ) %>% mutate(p_adj = p.adjust(p, method = "BH")) %>% arrange(p_adj) } # Create volcano plot for functional differences create_volcano_plot <- function(functional_differences, variable_label, gift_colors) { fc_threshold <- 0.2 fdr_threshold <- 0.05 plot_data <- functional_differences %>% mutate(func = substr(GIFT, 1, 3)) %>% mutate( p_adj_plot = ifelse(is.na(p_adj) | p_adj == 0, .Machine$double.xmin, p_adj), neglog10_fdr = -log10(p_adj_plot), hit = !is.na(p_adj) & p_adj < fdr_threshold & abs(diff) >= fc_threshold ) %>% mutate(func = ifelse(hit, func, "NS")) %>% filter(neglog10_fdr < 20) # Build color palette func_levels <- sort(unique(plot_data$func)) palette_df <- tibble(func = func_levels) %>% left_join( gift_colors %>% select(func = Code_function, Color), by = "func" ) %>% mutate( Color = case_when( func == "NS" & is.na(Color) ~ "grey70", is.na(Color) ~ "#999999", TRUE ~ Color ) ) color_values <- setNames(palette_df$Color, palette_df$func) plot_data %>% ggplot(aes(x = diff, y = neglog10_fdr, color = func)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.8, size = 2) + geom_vline(xintercept = c(-fc_threshold, fc_threshold), linetype = "dashed") + geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(fdr_threshold), linetype = "dashed") + ylim(0, 15) + xlim(-0.6, 0.6) + ggrepel::geom_text_repel( data = subset(plot_data, hit), aes(label = GIFT), size = 3, max.overlaps = 20, box.padding = 0.3, min.segment.length = 0 ) + scale_color_manual(values = color_values) + labs( x = "Mean difference (Positive − Negative)", y = expression(-log[10]("FDR (BH)")), color = "Group", subtitle = paste0("Thresholds: |diff| ≥ ", fc_threshold, ", FDR < ", fdr_threshold) ) + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) } # Aggregate beta coefficients by taxonomic level aggregate_by_taxonomy <- function(ci_data, tax_level = "phylum") { tax_sym <- rlang::sym(tax_level) ci_data %>% group_by(!!tax_sym) %>% summarise( mean_beta = mean(mean, na.rm = TRUE), q10 = stats::quantile(mean, 0.1, na.rm = TRUE), q90 = stats::quantile(mean, 0.9, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop" ) } # Map genomes to functional groups genome_func <- elements_response %>% dplyr::filter(value > 0) %>% dplyr::mutate(func = substr(GIFT, 1, 3)) %>% dplyr::distinct(genome, func) # Summarise by functional group func_summary <- genome_func %>% dplyr::left_join(genome_effects, by = "genome") %>% dplyr::group_by(func) %>% dplyr::summarise( n_genomes = sum(!is.na(mean)), mean_beta = mean(mean, na.rm = TRUE), q10_fun = stats::quantile(mean, 0.10, na.rm = TRUE), q90_fun = stats::quantile(mean, 0.90, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop" ) %>% dplyr::filter(n_genomes >= min_genomes) # Chapter 16 Predicted responses of highlighted functional groups Chapter 14 estimates a devil × temperature interaction for every genome. A few GIFT elements carry most of that signal, and stretching the interaction volcano to show them leaves the rest of the distribution hard to read. This chapter predicts how genomes that carry those elements respond, using the fitted model_final posterior. The manuscript figure uses the temperature prediction. Both that prediction and a second one, along predator density, are saved as supplementary figures. The two groups are the strongest interaction hits that also match the host story in the manuscript: Nitrogen compound degradation — betaine (D0608), nitrate (D0601) and creatinine (D0607) Amino acid degradation — histidine (D0512) Xenobiotic degradation is not included.
